title: Fierce and kind: Shankara
hookLine: the wild god drinks the poison no one else can touch, and his gentlest name is Shankara
carry: shiva's fierceness is for our well-being
tomorrow: who ties the soul, and who unties it?

cards: What do you call someone who frightens people and is still the one they run to? Shiva sits in cremation grounds, smeared with ash, a snake around his neck. Yesterday's list held Bhima, the fearsome one.
And yet, in the bhajans sung at temples and in living rooms, the names you'll hear most are soft ones. Shambho. Shankara.
Two names from the same hymn, and they don't sound frightening at all.

teach.b: Start with a story told to Hindu children everywhere. The gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality.
But before any treasure came up, out rose a poison so deadly it began to burn the worlds. Everyone ran. Everyone except Shiva, the wild one from the cremation grounds.

He took the poison and drank it. In many tellings Parvati caught his throat so it wouldn't go down, and it stayed there and turned his throat blue. That's why one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated.
The fearsome one was the only one who could hold the harm. Now hear two of his names.
Shankara: tradition explains it as the one who makes well-being, from sham, ease, and kara, the maker. Shambhu: the one from whom well-being comes.
A Vedic hymn still chanted in temples, the Shri Rudram, keeps the same pattern. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger and his arrows, not pretending he's harmless.
Deep in the hymn it turns, and bows to him as Shambhu, as Shankara, as Shiva, the auspicious one.

teach.h: THE RUDRAM: FROM ANGER TO NAMAH SHIVAYA.
teach.b: That's where the words namah shivaya are heard. So when the sahasranama puts Bhima, the fearsome, beside Shankara, it isn't confused.
This is the teaching: in Hindu devotion, Shiva's fierceness is for well-being. He burns what harms and swallows what would poison.

So when a family in a hospital waiting room quietly chants to Shiva, they aren't asking a frightening god to stay away. They're calling Shankara, the one who drank the poison so others wouldn't have to.

how: Devotees greet Shiva with names like Shambho, Shankara and Nilakantha in songs and chants; the Shri Rudram, with its line namah shivaya, is chanted in Shiva temples, especially during abhisheka, and Om Namah Shivaya is repeated as a mantra.

o: a hymn of Shiva's names, here gentle ones that mean well-being
a chant sung to keep Shiva's anger away from the house
a list of Shiva's battle titles, sung before a fight

games.q: the gentle names — tap the pairs.
p: the one from whom well-being comes
the Vedic hymn that turns from anger to Shiva

s: at the churning of the ocean, Shiva drank the poison that was burning the worlds
it stayed in his throat and turned it blue: Nilakantha.
the names Shambhu and Shankara appear in the Vedic Shri Rudram
deep in the hymn, it bows to him as Shambhu, Shankara and Shiva.
a gentle name cancels out a fierce one
the fierce one and the kind one are the same one; the gentle name says what the fierceness is for.

games.q: the churned ocean throws up a poison that's burning the worlds. the gods and demons run. who drinks it?
o: Shiva, the wild one from the cremation grounds.
nobody: they bury it in the sea.
games.why: Shiva drinks it and his throat turns blue. the fearsome one is the one who takes the harm: his fierceness is for well-being. that's Shankara.

practice: Sit tall and breathe out slowly. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya on each out-breath, the words heard in the Rudram, five or eleven times, picturing the blue throat that held the world's poison.
If you don't, bring to mind one fierce person in your life, and on each out-breath, name one thing their fierceness has protected.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's names from it: Shankara, the one who makes well-being, and Shambhu, from whom well-being comes. And the story behind them: Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Shankara, usually explained as the one who makes well-being; a name of Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: Shiva's fierceness is for our well-being. The blue throat shows it. See you tomorrow.
